activities.anchor: A vibrating body rarely moves as a single clean sine wave
activities.caption: file each instrument by the engine that drives it
activities.name: itEngineBuckets

config.prompt: Four solutions to one question: how do you make a body vibrate controllably? File each instrument:

items.label: guitar — plucked, bright attack, fast decay
clarinet — single reed, strong odd harmonics
trumpet — buzzing lips against a cup
timpani — a struck membrane in inharmonic partials
synthesizer — oscillators, an interface to a new engine

config.why: Keyboards are interfaces to other engines, not engines of their own — and percussion vibrates in the maths of a 2-D membrane, not a 1-D string.

activities.anchor: drums have no pitch at all
activities.caption: true or false — pitched percussion
activities.name: itDrumJudge

statements.s: A struck membrane vibrates in inharmonic partials, so the ear cannot lock onto one fundamental.
statements.why: Which is why drums read as 'unpitched' — the maths of a 2-D membrane, not a 1-D string.

statements.s: Marimba makers tune resonators beneath the bars to impose a pitch.
statements.why: The partials are there — the resonators pick one out.
Timpani are tuned percussion by any standard.

statements.s: A drum's sound contains no partials at all.
statements.why: The partials are there and inharmonic — the ear just cannot settle on a single fundamental.

activities.anchor: mixing engineers spend entire careers on that difference
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the doubling rule
activities.name: itDoublingSpot

config.prompt: An orchestration student's notes contain one faulty line — click it:
lines: A 'C on the violin' and 'a C on the trumpet' share the same fundamental frequency.
But they share nothing else: different spectral recipes and envelopes.
So doubling two instruments always reinforces the sound, whatever their partials do.
Partials that interleave reinforce; partials that collide fight — orchestration's first rule of doubling.
config.correction: Doubling reinforces only if the partials interleave — if they collide, the two instruments fight; that is orchestration's first rule of doubling.
config.why: Every judgement (warm, brassy, thin, round) is a statement about spectral recipe and envelope — two instruments at the same pitch are two different timbres.

config.prompt: A symphony orchestra is a machine built so one conductor can blend four recipe-families. Roughly how many string players does it carry?
config.why: Roughly sixty: 16 first violins, 14 seconds, 12 violas, 10 cellos, 8 basses — plus a dozen woodwinds, a dozen brass and five or so percussionists.
config.context: One conductor blending four recipe-families into a single evolving instrument.

activities.anchor: Ensembles are recipes for combining timbres
activities.caption: pair each named team with its sound-idea
activities.name: itEnsembleMatch

config.prompt: The named ensembles are sound-ideas, not just rosters. Pair each with its defining trait:

pairs.right: one family, four registers — blends and debates
the most portable ensemble on Earth, a four-octave vocabulary
tango built on the bandoneón's wheeze
soloist, tabla, and the tanpura drone as permanent tonal floor
gentle heterophony — everyone ornaments the same melody their own way

config.why: Every ensemble is a social contract written in timbre: who holds the pulse, who carries the tune, who paints the background.

activities.anchor: A worked contrast: take middle C on a violin
activities.caption: drag the divider — one string, two sounds
activities.name: itBowedCompare

config.prompt: Same string, same fundamental — technique is timbre. Drag the divider:

before.label: Bowed
before.text: The overtones hold in a steady choir — swell-and-hold; slide a mute under the bow and the note goes veiled.

after.label: Plucked
after.text: The pluck flashes a bright attack and decays — a harp hidden inside a violin; add sul ponticello and it turns glassy.

config.why: Four sounds, one string: pizzicato trades sustain for attack, and brass mutes or flutes' overblowing do the same job — the instrument is a family of timbres, not one.
